editorial:
Imagine waking up and realizing the police and doctors have spent years believing a man who confessed to murders he never actually committed. That is the crazy setup you get here. You follow Hannes Råstam, a reporter who just cannot let go of a story that feels wrong. He digs into the life of Thomas Quick, a man locked away in a psychiatric prison for crimes that seem impossible. The vibe is tense and frustrating because you can see the system failing right in front of you while the people in charge refuse to admit they made a mistake. It feels like a race against time to stop a huge lie from becoming the truth.

What really works is how the movie keeps you guessing about who is actually lying. The acting is solid, and the pacing moves quickly enough that you won't get bored. One downside is that it can feel a bit repetitive, but the shock of the real-life scandal makes up for it. If you love true crime stories, you should definitely check this out. You can stream it in 4K Ultra HD on Prime Video for a crisp look, or you might want to rent it on Apple TV for a movie night. If you are a collector, adding the 4K Blu-ray to your physical shelf is a great call.
endingExplained: The movie ends with the shocking reveal that Thomas Quick was a complete fraud. He did not have a repressed memory; he just made up all the murders to get attention and special treatment. Hannes proves that the police coached him into these fake confessions. In the end, Quick is released because he didn't actually kill anyone, but the legal system is left looking foolish for trusting a liar without any real evidence.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves true crime and legal dramas.
